newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD - AUGUST RESERVES SET TO DIP AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD - AUGUST RESERVES SET TO DIP AGAIN.

text.p: South Africa's foreign reserves are likely to decline again in August, but the tide may be turning with a steadier rand since mid-month starting to boost inflows, economists said.

Official gold and foreign exchange reserves, due on Friday, are seen falling to 10.1 billion rand in August from 10.37 billion in July, according to a consensus forecast of economists polled by Reuters.
"I think reserves during the month will have fallen below ten billion rand but they have probably since pulled back slightly," said Dennis Dykes, chief econimist at Nedcor bank.
"We've seen an improvement in the last part of the month."
Low reserves have been a focus for speculators selling rand in the belief the central Reserve Bank is running out of ammunition to defend the currency.

But in the last two weeks the rand has gained 10 cents from its all-time low of 4.59 against the dollar, forcing speculators long of dollars and short of rands to cut their positions. The currency was trading at its best level in three weeks on Friday.
Economists and foreign exchange dealers said there had been sizeable inflows this week from gold producers and other exporters seeking to convert overseas proceeds into rand.
By the end of July, which saw a decline of 0.9 billion rand, reserves represented just 1.1 months import cover.
The Reserve Bank also has some 15 billion rand in foreign credit lines which Governor Chris Stals said again last week he would use, if necessary, to provide liquidity for importers.

Herman van Papendorp, economist at SMK Securities, said net foreign sales of bonds and shares early in August would weigh on the reserve figure. This would be only partially offset by a better rand gold price, boosting the gold element.
But the position could improve from next month.
"Looking forward to September, I would guess the reserves situation will have stabilised and you may well see foreigners coming back into the market," he said.
Economists said encouraging trade and money supply data this week had boosted market sentiment, reassuring investors and easing pressure for an imminent Bank rate hike.
"It's been a good week, there is no question about it," said Nedcor's Dykes.
A sharp fall in the average three-month Treasury bill rate at Friday's auction to below Bank rate of 16 percent also soothed market nerves.
The average rate fell to 15.79 percent from 16.09 last week, as the central bank maintained a tight rein on supply with offers held at 600 million rand against the usual 900 million.

Stals made clear in his address to the Reserve Bank's annual meeting on Tuesday that he did not believe an interest rate increase was needed at present, although the situation remained finely balanced.

Since then things have been gone his way with a surge in the July trade surplus to an astonishing 2.58 billion rand and a fall in M3 growth easing Stals' two top concerns -- the current account deficit and ballooning money supply.

Analysts noted that the daily money market shortage remained very high at over nine billion rand, but said the situation should improve next week as the market put the traditional month-end squeeze behind it.
Internationally, U.S. payrolls, the most avidly watched economic figure in the world, will set financial markets alight once more in the coming week.

The National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) on Tuesday and housing figures on Thursday will act as warm-up acts before the jobs data on Friday. Markets are already nervous about the chance of higher U.S. interest rates and the coming data are seen as decisive.
"Payrolls loom largest," said Brian Venables, analyst at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.
He said the NAPM and housing completions -- especially after a recent surge in new home sales -- would be crucial as well.

If the reports combined to show a vibrant economy, a Federal Reserve rate rise at a September Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting will be back on the agenda, he said. "The one thing the Fed will try to avoid is a fiasco like we had in July," Venables said. In July, the Fed left rates unchanged at a FOMC meeting but markets were spooked when subsequent data showed plenty of economic muscle.
"The advantage this time is the FOMC is after the data rather than before," Venables said.
Simon Briscoe, economist at Nikko Europe in London, said payrolls would set the tone for bond markets.
"If you plot a chart of the long bond yield, the five or six lurches all occurred on payroll day," he said. He forecast a 225,000 rise compared with a 193,000 rise in July.
